title: CRLA/318/2018 of ANIL KISHOR TIWARI Vs STATE OF UTTARAKHAND

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Criminal Appeal No. 318 of 2018
Anil Kishore Tiwari ....... Appellant
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand .......Respondent
Mr. A.K. Sharma, Advocate for the appellant.
Mr. V.K. Gemini, Deputy Advocate General for the State.
Coram: Hon'ble Alok Singh, J.
 Hon'ble Ravindra Maithani, J.
Ravindra Maithani, J. (Oral)
The instant appeal has been preferred against the judgment
and order dated 18.09.2018, passed by learned District and Sessions
Judge, Gopeshwar, District Chamoli Garhwal in Sessions Trial No. 5 of
2015, State Vs. Anil Kishore Tiwari (for short "the case"), whereby the
appellant has been convicted under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to
imprisonment for life and with a fine of Rs.50,000/-.
2. Briefly stated, the case which is unfolded by the
prosecution is that, on 23.11.2014, at 10:30 in the morning, the appellant
lodged a missing report of his wife Smriti with Police Station Joshimath,
District Chamoli, Garhwal. According to it, his wife deceased Smriti
was missing since 22.11.2014. Based on this report, a Case Crime No.
35 of 2014, under Section 366 IPC was lodged. Appellant also informed
his father-in-law, PW1 Chandra Mani Nautiyal, about the missing of his
wife, the deceased. On 24.11.2014, at 01:30 PM, PW1 Chandra Mani
Nautiyal lodged a report with Police Station Joshimath. According to it,
appellant and the deceased were married on 20.11.2008, but she was

2
harassed for dowry by the appellant and other in-laws. Out of the
wedlock, two daughters were born. She was harassed and taunted for not
delivering a baby boy. The appellant also doubted her fidelity and filed a
suit for divorce on that false ground. The deceased had informed all
these facts to PW1 Chandra Mani Nautiyal. He consoled his daughter
saying that in due course of time, things will be normal. According to
the report, the appellant and his family members killed the deceased.
Based on this report, Case Crime No. 36 of 2014, under Sections 498-A
and 304-B IPC was lodged and investigation carried out.
3. The dead body of the deceased was found and an inquest
was prepared by PW15 C.S. Vashistha, Naib Teshsildar on 25.11.2014.
The body was in three pieces. Both the legs were separated from the
remaining body. PW10 Dr. Manoj Sharma alongwith Dr. Praveen
Shrivastava conducted the post mortem and opined that though the cause
of the death could not be commented by certainty because body was
severely mutilated, but to the best of the knowledge of the doctors, who
conducted the post mortem, it is due to asphyxia, as a result of ante
mortem throttling. During investigation, site plan of the place of incident
was prepared. A motorcycle was also taken into custody and charge-sheet was submitted against the appellant under Sections 302, 366 IPC.
On 11.03.2015, charges under Sections 302, 498-A and 304-B IPC were
framed against the appellant, to which he denied and claimed trial.
4. Prosecution in order to prove the case, examined as many
as, 15 witnesses, namely PW1 Chandra Mani Nautiyal, PW2 Smt.

3
Pushpa Devi, PW3 Smt. Rajani Devi, PW4 Smt. Sulochana Pawar, PW5
Durga Singh, PW6 Sobat Singh Pawar, PW7 Virendra Singh Panwar,
PW8 Const. Vikash Chandra, PW9 H.C. Mohan Singh Bisht, PW10 Dr.
Manoj Sharma, PW11 C.O. Jagdish Chandra Yadav, PW12 C.O.
Bhoopal Singh Rawat, PW13 Harendra Singh Bisht, PW14 Dy. S.P.
Swatantra Kumar Singh and PW15 Chandra Shekhar Vasisth.
5. The appellant was examined under Section 313 of the Code
of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as "the Code").
According to the appellant, he has been falsely implicated in the case.
The appellant in his examination under Section 313 of the Code
admitted the statements of various witnesses, it would be referred to at
an appropriate stage.
6. In answer to question no. 34, the appellant would say that
his wife was erratic and she was dangerous to herself and when he
informed her parents and sent a notice to his in-laws, they in reply told
him that she is no more their responsibility and he had to take care of the
deceased. According to the appellant, his in-laws has destroyed his life.
7 Heard learned counsel for the appellant, learned counsel for
the State and perused the record.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant would argue that this is a
case based on circumstantial evidence, but the chain of events is not
complete to bring home the guilt; FIR is delayed; appellant himself had
informed his father-in-law about the missing of the deceased. It is

4
argued that prosecution utterly failed to establish the chain of events and
the benefit of doubt ought to have been given to the appellant. It is also
argued that appellant has two daughters back at home and appellant is
the only person to take care of them, who are aged ten years and six
years respectively.
9. In support of his contention, learned counsel for the
appellant placed reliance upon the principles of law, as laid down in the
case of Rambraksh @ Jalim Vs. State of Chhattisgarh, (2016) 12 SCC
251. In this case, Hon'ble Supreme Court, inter alia, held that last seen
theory in itself cannot be a basis for conviction. The Court observed as
hereunder:-
"12. It is trite law that a conviction cannot be recorded against
the accused merely on the ground that the accused was last seen with
the deceased. In other words, a conviction cannot be based on the
only circumstance of last seen together. Normally, last seen theory
comes into play where the time gap, between the point of time when
the accused and the deceased were seen last alive and when the
deceased is found dead, is so small that possibility of any person
other than the accused being the perpetrator of the crime becomes
impossible. To record a conviction, the last seen together itself would
not be sufficient and the prosecution has to complete the chain of
circumstances to bring home the guilt of the accused."
10. On the other hand, learned State counsel would argue that
prosecution has been able to prove the charges against the appellant; he
was last seen with the deceased, his wife; appellant gave false
explanation about the missing of his wife; the conduct of the appellant is
highly doubtful; Learned State counsel would argue that the medical
evidence also supports the ocular evidence and it is a case proved
beyond reasonable doubt. Learned court below did not commit any error
in convicting the appellant, therefore, appeal deserves to be dismissed.

5
11. There are three sets of witnesses. PW1 Chandra Mani
Nautiyal, and PW2 Pushpa Devi are parents of the deceased. PW5
Durga Singh, PW6 Sobat Singh Panwar, PW7 Virendra Singh Panwar
and PW8 Constable, Vikas Chandra have stated as to what had
happened in the late evening on 22.11.2014. According to them, they
were told on that day that the wife of the appellant is missing from a
place called Bhanerpani, which is at a distance of about 2-3 kms from
their village. They made a search but could not trace the deceased. Their
statements would be examined at a later stage.
12. PW9 Constable Mohan Singh Bisht proved the entries of
the General Diary, regarding lodging of this case as well as lodging of
the missing report by the appellant on 23.11.2014 at 10:30 AM at Police
Station Joshimath. PW15 Chandra Shekhar Vashistha was Naib
Tehsildar at the relevant time, when inquest was prepared.
13. PW10 Dr. Manoj Sharma, conducted the post mortem,
PW11 Jagdish Chandra Yadav, PW 12, Bhupal Singh Rawat, PW13
Harendra Singh Bisht and PW14 Swatantra Kumar Sing are the
Investigating Officers.
14. According to PW1 Chandra Mani Nautiyal, his daughter
and the appellant were married on 23.11.2008. Out of the wedlock, two
daughters were born. The appellant doubted the fidelity of his wife and
also gave a notice to that effect to this witness, asking him to take back
the deceased. According to PW1 Chandra Mani Nautiyal, thereafter, he

6
approached the appellant. Appellant assured him not to reply the notice
saying that in due course of time, things would be normal. According to
PW1, on 23.11.2014, at about 10:00 in the morning, appellant gave him
a telephonic call and informed that the deceased went missing from the
previous night. The appellant informed that she had gone in some
vehicle, which had come at his home to take her. This witness alongwith
the family members, visited the appellant's house. On 24.11.2014, he
lodged a report and thereafter, went at the place, where the dead body of
the deceased was recovered.
15. PW2 Pushpa Devi is mother of the deceased Smriti. She
states that the appellant would torture his wife and doubted her fidelity.
She also states about the telephonic calls made by the appellant about
the missing of her daughter.
16. PW3 Smt. Rajani Devi and PW4 Smt. Sulochana Panwar
are two women of the same village. According to them, they saw the
appellant with his wife on a motorcycle going towards Gopeshwar and
thereafter, they did not see the deceased and the next day, they came to
know that the deceased Smriti is missing. Both have not categorically
stated about the date, but PW4 Smt. Sulochana Panwar states that it was
a Saturday. The fact remains that 22.11.2014 was a Saturday.
17. According to PW5 Durga Singh, on 22.11.2014, at about
08:30 in the evening, the brother of the appellant Sunil came to him and
told that the appellant's motorcycle met with an accident, near a place

7
called Bhanerpani and the wife of appellant is not traceable. Thereafter,
according to this witness, he alongwith other villagers went to the Police
Chowki and from there, they visited the place called Bhanerpani. The
appellant's motorcycle was parked there, but appellant was not present.
It was dark. They searched for the wife of the appellant, the deceased,
but could not trace her. According to PW5 Durga Singh, on the next
day, the appellant's brother had taken the motorcycle back at home,
which was subsequently taken into custody by the Police. PW6 Sobat
Singh Panwar, PW7 Virendra Singh Panwar and PW8 Constable Vikas
Chandra all have corroborated the statement of PW5 Durga Singh.
18. Statement of PW7 Virendra Singh Panwar is little more
important, because according to him, on that day, the appellant had
telephoned him at about 08:30 PM and informed that while appellant
was returning from Gopeshwar, at a place called Bhanerpani his wife
went missing. Thereafter, this witness joined the search party.
19. PW9 Head Constable, Mohan Singh Bisht proved the chik
FIR and the entries in the general diary. According to PW9 Mohan
Singh Bisht, on 23.11.2014, at 10:30 AM, the appellant had lodged a
report about missing of his wife, which was registered in General Diary
Report No. 60. He has also proved this general diary entry.
20. According to PW10 Dr. Manoj Sharma on 26.11.2014, he
conducted post mortem of the deceased alongwith Dr. Praveen
Shrivastava and on external examination found the following injuries on
the person of the deceased:-

8
1. Abraded contusion of size 3 x 1 cm are seen on both side of
neck laterally, slight clotted blood remanant are seen.
2. Large open wound is seen involving the whole forehead and
anterior part of skull with fracture and disfiguration of the
skull and facial bones. Skull is open from the frontal part,
both eye globes & brain is absent.
3. Both jaw are fractured & are exposed with missing of teeths.
4. A large clear edge open wound extending from right side of
tip of chest to the nipple of left breast is seen, underlying
bony cage is open so that thoracic cavity is exposed, lungs are
found lying freely while heart is absent.
5. Clear edge open wound involving the whole circumference of
the abdomen, at the level of ILIAC region is seen so that
whole abdomen cavity is exposed but no viscera is found
inside it.
6. Clear edge wound is seen involving the whole circumference
of the upper part of the thigh or both lower limbs exposing the
tissue underneath & bones, both lower limbs are separated
from, the trunk & external genitalia are absent only part of
skin having pubic hairs are seen attached.
7. A clear edge wound is seen involving the anterior part of the
left arm in middle 1/3RD with under neath bone is broken &
exposed from the wound.
8. A clear edge open wound is seen on the antero midial size of
the left lower leg, under lying bones are fractured & exposed.
9. A cut wound of size 6 x 3 cm is seen on the lateral side of
right foot is fracture of the under lying bone which are
exposed, tailing of wound is seen on lower side.
10. A clear edge large open wound is seen on the right side of the
face involving the cheek.
21. In an internal examination of the dead body, PW10 Dr.
Manoj Shama has opined that the bones of skull and face were fractured;
brain and its membrane were missing; lungs were filled with blood;
tongue was lacerated; membranes were missing.
22. According to PW10 Dr. Manoj Sharma, the cause of death
to the best of his knowledge was asphyxia due to throttling. This witness
proved the post mortem report.
23. PW14 Deputy Superintendent of Police, Swatantra Kumar
Singh is the first Investigating Officer, who prepared the site plan Ex A-9. PW 12 C.O., Bhoopal Singh Rawat is the second Investigating

9
Officer, who also prepared a site plan and took into custody the
motorcycle. PW11 Jagdish Chandra Yadav is the third Investigating
Officer. According to him, during investigation, he did not find offences
under Sections 304-B and 498-A IPC, therefore, the investigation was
transferred. PW13 Harendra Singh Bisht is the Investigating Officer,
who finally conducted the investigation and submitted the charge-sheet.
According to PW15 Chandra Shekhar Vasistha, he was directed to
prepare the inquest, which he did prepare on 25.11.2014. He proved the
inquest and other documents relating to postmortem.
24. Undoubtedly, this is a case based on circumstantial
evidence. Law of circumstantial evidence is well settled. The chain
should be complete, which may draw an irresistible conclusion that it is
the accused and accused only, who has committed the offence. In the
case of Rambraksh @ Jalim (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court, inter-alia, held that the last seen theory itself would not be sufficient for
recording a conviction. The prosecution has to prove the complete chain
of events to bring home the guilt of the accused.
25. In the cases of circumstantial evidence, it is also settled
legal position that motive plays a very important role. In the instant case,
motive and acrimony between the parties is established. The appellant
was not in good terms with his wife. PW1 Chandra Mani Nautiyal has
stated that, doubting her fidelity, a divorce suit was filed by the
appellant and a notice was also given to this witness, requiring him to
take back the deceased.

10
26. Be it as it may, it is well established by the prosecution that
the appellant was not happy with his wife, the deceased. They had very
strained relationship. The divorce suit was filed. It's a motive, which is
established and proved.
27. On 22.11.2014, the appellant took his wife Smriti, the
deceased alongwith him on a motorcycle and since thereafter, nobody
had seen her. The deceased went missing. She was seen last time with
the appellant. It was, in fact, appellant, who had to tell as to where the
deceased had gone.
28. In the cases of last seen theory, the proximity of time and
distance is also very relevant. In the instant case, both are proximate. On
22.11.2014, at 10.30 AM, the appellant took his wife with him and in
the evening, on the same day, he informs that the deceased has gone
missing. There are two versions to it. According to PW5 Durga Singh,
the brother of the appellant would inform him, on that day, that
appellant's motorcycle had met with an accident, a fact which was not
true, because when PW5 Durga Singh alongwith PW6 Sobat Singh
Pawar, PW7 Virendra Singh Panwar and PW8 Const. Vikash Chandra
visited the place, they did not see any accident, instead motorcycle was
intact. Except PW7 Virendra Singh Panwar, none of these witnesses had
seen the appellant on that day.
29. PW7 Virendra Singh Panwar is very important witness in
this case. He receives a call from the appellant himself, informing him

11
that when he was returning from Gopeshwar, near a place called
Bhanerpani his wife went missing. How she went missing? What
happened at the place called Bhanerpani? It may be noted here that
according to PW5 Durga Singh, the appellant's brother Sunil had
informed him at the same time that appellant's motorcycle had met with
an accident. Appellant himself did not join the search party.
30. The things did not stop here. On 23.11.2014 in the
morning, appellant informs the police that since the late evening of
22.11.2014, his wife is missing. The prosecution should have proved the
report given by the appellant at the Police Station, which they did not
do. PW9 Constable M.S. Bisht proved the general diary entry of Police
Station Joshimath. According to it, on 22.11.2014, the deceased had
gone missing from her house. In this general diary report, which is
Ex.A-4, the appellant did not inform the police that, from a place called
Bhanerpani, his wife went missing, instead, he informs that from his
house she went missing. So, there are three versions now. According to
PW5 Durga Singh, the brother of the appellant informs him that the
motorcycle of the appellant met with an accident at a place called
Bhanerpani. Secondly, according to PW7 Virendra Singh Panwar, he
was informed by the appellant himself at about 08:30, in the evening,
that while returning from Gopeshwar at a place called Bhanerpani his
wife went missing. As stated, it is not told how she went missing. What
has happened at a place called Bhanerpani, because motorcycle has not
met with an accident, it was intact. It was taken back home, the next day
by the brother of the appellant, as stated by the witnesses. And thirdly,

12
the appellant lodges a report at Police Station on 23.11.2014 at 10:30
AM, stating therein that the deceased went missing from his house since
previous night. These are three stories. The fact was within the special
knowledge of the appellant because the deceased, his wife was with
him. He was the best person to tell as to how and under what
circumstances, from a place called Bhanerpani his wife went missing.
He gave many explanations of it, at least three, as stated hereinbefore.
31. The dead body of the deceased was recovered; it was in
three pieces; lungs were congested; doctor has opined that though it was
very tough to give any opinion about the cause of death but according to
PW10 Dr. Manoj Sharma, the cause of death was asphyxia due to ante
mortem throttling. The death was not suicidal or accidental, instead
according to PW10 Manoj Sharma, it was homicidal. Appellant was
with her. It is the appellant, who took the deceased with him on
22.11.2014 from his house towards Gopeshwar. He was spotted going
on a motorcycle, as stated by the witnesses. Site plan Ex. A6 has been
proved by PW12 Bhoopal Singh Rawat, the Investigating Officer. The
topography of the place, from where the deceased went missing and the
place from where her dead body recovered is very important. It is a
highway, which leads towards Joshimath. PW8 Constable Vikash
Chandra has described it. From the road down towards the river, it is
steep rock. Motorcycle of the appellant was on the motor road and the
dead body was recovered below it from the river. There is definitely
proximity of place as well as of time because dead body was recovered
on 25.11.2014 from the river. In the late evening, the appellant returns

13
home and gives a different story about the whereabouts of the deceased.
There was no accident of the motorcycle, as told to PW5 Durga Singh.
The deceased did not go missing from her house on 22.11.2014, as
informed by the appellant himself to the police, and as stated by PW9
Constable M.S. Bisht. She was not traced at a place called Bhanerpani.
Though inferences should not be drawn on the basis of conduct but at
times it speaks louder than spoken words. The wife of a person is
missing but he did not join, the search party to trace her. The death of
the deceased was not accidental, it was homicidal. These all events
together makes a complete chain. The circumstances are complete and
they make only one and one conclusion, which is irresistible that it is the
appellant and the appellant alone, who killed his wife, Smriti.
32. Reference can be made to various replies given by the
appellant in his examination under Section 313 of the Code. The legal
position is settled that the statement given by an accused under Section
313 of the Code is not evidence. However, false explanation given by
the accused can always be taken into consideration to fortify the finding
of guilt already recorded. A false defence may be called to add only to
lend assurance to the Court.
33. In his reply to question no.12, under Section 313 of the
Code, the appellant admits that on 22.04.2014, he took his wife on the
motorcycle with him. He admits the correctness of the statements made
by PW3 Smt. Pushpa Devi and PW4 Smt. Sulochana Panwar. In answer
to question no.3, the appellant admitted that he had filed the divorce suit

14
against the deceased, but according to him, it was not on the ground of
non-fidelity, instead due to her conduct, he had filed a divorce suit. In
answer to question no.34, the appellant has categorically stated that he
was upset due to conduct of the deceased and in the last sentence in
answer to this question, he says that his in-laws have destroyed his life.
Appellant in answer to question no.16 also admitted that he on
22.04.2014 at 8:30 PM informed PW7 Virendra Singh Panwar that his
wife went missing from Bhanerpani. He admits correctness of the
statement of PW7 Virendra Singh Panwar. If the wife of the appellant
had gone missing, why did he not join the search? To it, the appellant in
answer to question no.17 in his examination under Section 313 of the
Code, when he says that he stayed back at home to look after the small
daughters.
34. The above statements made by the appellant in his
examination under Section 313 of the Code, definitely lend assurance to
the Court that the appellant killed his wife, deceased Smriti.
35. In view of the foregoing discussion, this Court is of the
view that the prosecution has been able to prove the case against the
appellant beyond reasonable doubt. Learned court below rightly
convicted and sentenced the appellant under Section 302 IPC.
Therefore, the appeal deserves to be dismissed.
36. The appeal is dismissed accordingly.
(Ravindra Maithani, J.) (Alok Singh, J.)
 03.09.2019
Shubham
